outcome: Not settled for general graphs as of 11 October 2026: no counterexample and no proof that the representation number is at most floor(n/2) appears in any source I could read. The one new event that bears directly on the bullet since 26 January 2024 is Colbrook and Drysdale (arXiv 2609.35842, 24 Sep 2026), which settles the bipartite class (every bipartite graph on N ≥ 9 vertices has representation number at most ⌈N/4⌉), with ChatGPT-assisted steps declared by the authors; two Hefty–Horn–Muir–Owens papers on lower bounds (EJC 2024, JCTA 2026) could bear on general graphs but their full texts were not readable, so that remains unverified.
problem_asks: (1) Existence: for a given n (or for some n; the bullet does not say which), is there a graph G on n vertices whose representation number R(G) exceeds floor(n/2)? R(G) is the least k such that G is represented by a word over its vertices in which each letter occurs exactly k times and two distinct letters alternate exactly when they are adjacent; because k-representable implies (k+1)-representable, 'requires more than floor(n/2) copies' is read as R(G) > floor(n/2). (2) Scope: every graph on n vertices, with no restriction to bipartite, triangle-free, or any other class. (3) Word-representability: the bullet does not say what to do with graphs that have no representation at all (non-word-representable graphs, with R = infinity); a literal reading would count them. (4) The bullet asks only for the existence question with floor(n/2) as the threshold; it does not ask for the exact maximum representation number of each n.

events.what_happened: Halldórsson, Kitaev and Pyatkin, 'On representable graphs, semi-transitive orientations, and the representation numbers', arXiv:0810.0310 (1 Oct 2008; one version). The abstract (opened) states that 'the representation number of a graph on n nodes is at most n' and that the bound 'is tight up to a constant factor, as we present a graph whose representation number is n/2'. Search excerpts, not checked in the PDF (not extractable), place the n/2 family in a theorem numbered 15: the crown graph H_{k,k} plus an all-adjacent vertex, with representation number k = floor(n/2) on n = 2k+1 vertices.
events.revisions: v1 only (1 Oct 2008) per the arXiv abstract page. The same authors' 2015 preprint (arXiv:1501.07108) and its 2016 journal version state the general upper bound as 2n, not n. No withdrawal or correction notice was found, and the record does not show whether the 2008 bound was withdrawn, corrected or dropped.
events.delivers: Claims R(G) ≤ n for every word-representable graph G on n vertices (a bound the 2015/2016 versions do not repeat). Exhibits a family with R = n/2, which for odd n is floor(n/2) (per excerpts). Establishes that some n-vertex graphs have representation number about n/2, which makes floor(n/2) the natural frontier.
events.remains: Whether any graph on n vertices has R > floor(n/2). The abstract does not address it. If the claimed bound R ≤ n were right, it would cap R at n, leaving the gap (floor(n/2), n] open.
events.directly_checkable: The n/2 family is an explicit graph (crown graph with an added all-adjacent vertex); its representation number can be checked by computer for small k. The authors' check was not read.
events.doubts: (1) The 2008 bound R ≤ n is inconsistent with the 2n bound the same authors state in 2015; the record cannot say which is correct or whether the 2008 claim was retracted. (2) Theorem 15 and the family's identity come from search excerpts, since the PDF was not extractable.
events.direction: Consistent with the question's threshold: it exhibits graphs with R about n/2 and makes no claim that exceeds floor(n/2). Its upper bound n is a claim about a different quantity and does not settle whether floor(n/2) is exceeded.
events.object: A family of graphs with representation number n/2 (for odd n, floor(n/2)): the crown graph H_{k,k} (K_{k,k} minus a perfect matching, 2k vertices) with one added all-adjacent vertex, giving G_k on 2k+1 vertices with representation number k (per search excerpts of Theorem 15; not read in the paper). Explicit, not existential. Does not exceed floor(n/2).

events.what_happened: Halldórsson, Kitaev and Pyatkin, 'Semi-transitive orientations and word-representable graphs', arXiv:1501.07108 (submitted 28 Jan 2015; one version, submitter Kitaev), published Discrete Applied Mathematics 201 (2016) 164–171, DOI 10.1016/j.dam.2015.07.033 (journal details from a Strathclyde record in search results). The abstract (opened) states that the representation number of a word-representable graph on n vertices is at most 2n, 'while there exist graphs for which it is n/2', and that the bound is 'tight up to a constant factor'. Wikipedia's article and Kitaev's 2017 survey (both opened) cite the journal version for the bound 'each non-complete word-representable graph G is 2(n − κ(G))-representable', κ(G) the maximum clique size; since κ ≥ 2 for a non-complete graph with an edge, this gives 2n − 4. The paper's PDF was not extractable, so that bound is from the secondary sources.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (28 Jan 2015) per the abstract page. Journal version DAM 201 (2016) 164–171.
events.delivers: Characterises word-representability by semi-transitive orientations. Upper bound R ≤ 2n (abstract) and, per secondary sources, R ≤ 2(n − κ) ≤ 2n − 4 for non-complete graphs. Lower bound family with R = n/2 (abstract). Not a resolution of the question: the gap between n/2 and 2n − 4 is left open.
events.remains: Whether any graph on n vertices has R > floor(n/2). The upper bound leaves a gap of roughly n to 2n − 4 above the best-known family.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in DAM 201 (2016) 164–171 (per the Strathclyde record in search results; the referee process itself is not visible)

events.doubts: The 2n bound replaced the 2008 preprint's n (see the 2008 event), and the 2(n − κ) form is taken from secondary sources only (Wikipedia citing the 2016 paper; Kitaev's survey, Theorem 32), not read in the paper itself.
events.direction: Neutral to the question. Supplies the n/2 benchmark and an upper bound well above it.

events.what_happened: Glen, Kitaev and Pyatkin, 'On the representation number of a crown graph', arXiv:1609.00674 (submitted 2 Sep 2016; one version), published Discrete Applied Mathematics 244 (2018) 89–93, DOI 10.1016/j.dam.2018.03.013 (journal details from search results). The arXiv abstract (opened) states that for n ≥ 5 the crown graph H_{n,n} (K_{n,n} minus a perfect matching, 2n vertices) has representation number ⌈n/2⌉, that this completely solves Problem 7.4.2 of Kitaev and Lozin's book Words and Graphs (2015), and that it answers Problem 7.2.7 negatively. The paper's introduction (opened, HTML) says non-bipartite graphs obtained from crown graphs by adding an all-adjacent vertex 'require roughly twice as long words'.
events.revisions: v1 only per the arXiv abstract page; journal version DAM 244 (2018).
events.delivers: Exact value of R for crowns: R(H_{n,n}) = ⌈n/2⌉ for n ≥ 5. Here N = 2n vertices and R = ⌈N/4⌉, far below floor(N/2). This is a bipartite family that does not exceed the threshold. It does not address graphs in general.
events.remains: All graphs on n vertices (the bullet is about every graph, not crowns). The crown-plus-apex family, which reaches floor(n/2) at odd order according to secondary sources, is the closest known match to the threshold.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published in DAM 244 (2018) 89–93 (per search results; the paper was not opened in the journal version)

events.directly_checkable: The crown graph H_{n,n} is explicit, and its representation number can be checked by computer for small n. The proof was not read.
events.direction: Consistent with the question: a bipartite family whose representation number is ⌈N/4⌉ is far below floor(N/2).
events.object: Explicit crown graphs H_{n,n} (K_{n,n} minus a perfect matching) with R = ⌈n/2⌉ for n ≥ 5 (value from the abstract; the proof was not read). Not a counterexample: R = ⌈n/2⌉ = ⌈N/4⌉ for N = 2n vertices.

events.what_happened: Akgün, Gent, Kitaev and Zantema, 'Solving computational problems in the theory of word-representable graphs', arXiv:1808.01215 (submitted 3 Aug 2018; one version), Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019) Article 19.2.5. The abstract (opened) reports exhaustive computation: enumeration of connected non-word-representable graphs up to 11 vertices (3 CPU years, which led to a correction of a published result), a 'distribution of k-representable graphs on at most 9 vertices', and 'a new graph on 9 vertices with high representation number'. Search excerpts of the full text (PDF not extractable) add: the 9-vertex word-representable graphs with representation number 4 are G_4 (known) and a new graph J_4 (a non-comparability graph); no word-representable graph on at most 9 vertices has representation number above 4; and the authors say this 'may suggest that Conjecture 2 might not be true'. Conjecture 2, per excerpts, is Kitaev's conjecture that the crown with an apex, G_n, has the highest representation number among graphs on 2n+1 vertices.
events.revisions: v1 only per the arXiv abstract page; journal version JIS 22 (2019) 19.2.5.
events.delivers: Finite instances: exhaustive computation for graphs on at most 9 vertices. Per excerpts, every word-representable graph on at most 9 vertices has R ≤ 4. That is at most floor(n/2) at n = 8 and 9 only; for n ≤ 7, floor(n/2) ≤ 3, so R ≤ 4 does not by itself establish R ≤ floor(n/2) there. The per-n maxima tables were not read. Finite instances of a universal claim do not resolve it (§2.1).
events.remains: All n ≥ 10, and the per-n threshold for n ≤ 7 and 8 (the per-n maxima were not read).

machine_checked.system: Exhaustive computer enumeration with semi-transitive orientation tests (the authors' own code; not a proof assistant)

events.directly_checkable: The graph J_4 (9 vertices, non-comparability, R = 4) is a finite object that could be checked by computer; its construction was not read.
events.doubts: The enumeration led to a correction of a published result (per the abstract), so the computational pipeline has already been revised once. The per-n tables and the J_4 construction were not read.
events.direction: Consistent with the question: no counterexample for graphs up to 9 vertices. J_4 attains floor(9/2) = 4 exactly, so it is not a counterexample.
events.object: J_4, a 9-vertex non-comparability graph with representation number 4 = floor(9/2) (per search excerpts), and G_4, a comparability graph on 9 vertices with the same value. Neither exceeds the threshold.

events.what_happened: Mozhui and Krishna, 'On the representation number of bipartite graphs', arXiv:2109.03458 (submitted 8 Sep 2021; one version; comment says RAMiCS 2021). The abstract (opened) gives a polynomial-time relabeling algorithm producing 'an upper bound for the representation number of bipartite graphs', and an upper bound on poset dimension for bipartite-derived posets. It states that 'it was conjectured that the representation number of bipartite graphs on n vertices is at most n/4', without naming the conjecturer. The 2025 follow-up (see the next event) attributes the conjecture to Glen et al.
events.revisions: v1 only per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: An upper bound for representation numbers of bipartite graphs, not stated explicitly in the abstract. Restricted to bipartite graphs. The n/4 conjecture is not proved here.
events.remains: The bipartite conjecture, and the whole question for non-bipartite graphs.
events.direction: Restricted to bipartite graphs; consistent with the question, which is about an upper threshold.

events.what_happened: Mozhui and Krishna, 'On the Conjecture of the Representation Number of Bipartite Graphs', arXiv:2506.01057 (submitted 1 Jun 2025; one version, v1, submitter K. V. Krishna). The abstract (opened) states that every bipartite graph is (1 + ⌈m/2⌉)-representable, m the size of the smaller partite set; when m is odd the bound drops to ⌈m/2⌉. So the Glen et al. conjecture (R ≤ ⌈(m+n)/4⌉ for bipartite graphs with partite sets of sizes m and n, m + n ≥ 9) holds for all bipartite graphs except those with both partite sets of equal, even size. For that remaining class the authors prove the conjecture for subclasses, using a neighbourhood-inclusion-graph approach. Search excerpts say the representation numbers are known for all bipartite graphs with at most nine vertices (not verified in full text).
events.revisions: v1 only (1 Jun 2025) per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: For bipartite graphs with smaller part m: R ≤ 1 + ⌈m/2⌉. Since m ≤ floor(N/2), this gives R ≤ floor(N/2) for N ≥ 4 (my arithmetic from the abstract's bound; the paper does not state it). The Glen et al. conjecture is settled for all bipartite graphs outside the equal-even-parts class, and proved for subclasses inside it.
events.remains: Non-bipartite graphs entirely. Bipartite graphs with equal, even partite sets, except the proven subclasses.
events.direction: Restricted to bipartite graphs; its bound is consistent with the question's threshold for N ≥ 4.

events.what_happened: Colbrook and Drysdale, 'Crown graphs maximise the representation number of bipartite graphs', arXiv:2609.35842 (submitted 24 Sep 2026, math.CO, cross-listed cs.DM; one version). The abstract (opened, HTML) states that every bipartite graph on N ≥ 9 vertices has representation number at most ⌈N/4⌉, and that this settles the conjecture that crowns maximise the representation number among bipartite graphs of the same order (Corollary 1.2; H_{n,n} attains the bound by equation (1.1)). The proof builds on a construction of Mozhui and Krishna and reduces to an ordering problem on neighbourhoods. Two finite cases (six and eight vertices per part) are settled by Boolean unsatisfiability certificates, and the main theorem and crown corollary are formalised in Lean 4. The AI declaration in Section 6.2 is recorded under ai.
events.revisions: v1 only (24 Sep 2026) per the arXiv abstract page. No v2 page was found (arxiv.org/abs/2609.35842v2 returned 404).
events.delivers: Bipartite class only: every bipartite graph on N ≥ 9 vertices has R ≤ ⌈N/4⌉. Since ⌈N/4⌉ ≤ floor(N/2) for N ≥ 9, no bipartite graph on N ≥ 9 vertices is a counterexample to the bullet. Combined with the Mozhui–Krishna bound (my arithmetic), no bipartite graph on N ≥ 4 vertices is a counterexample. This is a restriction to a class, not a resolution of the general question (§2.1).
events.remains: Every non-bipartite graph, at every order. Whether a non-bipartite graph on n vertices exceeds floor(n/2) is not addressed.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (version 4.33.1 per the repository README) with Lean Comparator; finite cases checked by Boolean unsatisfiability certificates in the repository's validation scripts

events.directly_checkable: The crown extremality and the finite certificates are computational, and the repository contains the certificate data and validators (per the README). The ordering argument is not hand-checkable in a short form.
events.doubts: (1) Single version, posted 17 days before this record; no peer review and no independent reading found (no blog post, review, or citing paper in search). (2) Model assistance is declared for the approach, the classification, the odd-part argument, the finite certificates, and the Lean formalisation (see ai). The authors state they reviewed all content and take responsibility for it. (3) The Lean repository's owner is a GitHub user, miinadietrich, whose relation to the authors is not stated; the sorry-free status is taken from the README's statement that the proof closure uses only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and the Lean files themselves were not read. (4) MathWorld's entry repeats the claim; it is a reference summary, not a check.
events.direction: Cuts against bipartite counterexamples to the threshold for N ≥ 9: it bounds bipartite R by ⌈N/4⌉, below floor(N/2). Silent on non-bipartite graphs.

systems.what_it_did: Discussions with the authors from which the approach arose; the paper does not say which step the discussions produced beyond the approach as a whole.
systems.basis_quote: This approach arose through discussions between the authors and ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.6
systems.what_it_did: (a) Co-source of the approach, per the joint sentence above. (b) The obstruction classification (the paper's wording: 'The classification also emerged from discussions between the authors and ChatGPT 5.6, after the authors directed attention to the implications between the possible assignments of the unspecified ranks.'). (c) Through Codex, assistance with combinatorial counting and with constructing and verifying the finite computational certificates.
systems.basis_quote: We used ChatGPT 5.6 through Codex to assist with combinatorial counting and with the construction and verification of the finite computational certificates.

systems.name: ChatGPT 6
systems.what_it_did: Discussions 'towards the remaining odd part sizes', from the classification onward (per the sentence below), and, through Codex and after the manuscript was developed, assistance with a Lean formalisation of the proof. The Lean work is formalisation of an argument already proven, which by itself would not count; the odd-part discussions are the load-bearing part.
systems.basis_quote: Building on this classification, the authors directed further discussions with ChatGPT 6 towards the remaining odd part sizes. After developing the manuscript, we used ChatGPT 6 through Codex to assist with a Lean formalisation of the proof.

events.what_happened: Hefty, Horn, Muir and Owens, 'Word-Representable Graphs: Orientations, Posets, and Bounds', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 31(4) (2024) #P4.2, DOI 10.37236/12806. Dates from search results: submitted 16 Feb 2024, accepted 6 Sep 2024, published 4 Oct 2024. No arXiv preprint was found. The abstract (opened on the journal page) says the paper uses tools from posets, Ramsey theory, finite geometry and probabilistic methods, and 'settle[s] a number of open problems in the field, regarding both the existence and length of word-representations for various classes of graphs'. Search excerpts of the full text (the PDFs were not extractable) add: two new lower bounds on the representation number of a graph, a counting bound (Corollary 20) and a bound from the structure of orientations (Theorem 25); R of the n-cube is O(log n / log log n); bipartite graphs of maximum degree Δ have R = O(Δ log^(1+o(1)) Δ); triangle-free graphs of large chromatic number with R = O(√n) exist.
events.revisions: No arXiv or other earlier public version was found. The date given is the journal publication date, used because nothing earlier was found; the first public version may be earlier (submission 16 Feb 2024).
events.delivers: Per the abstract, lower bounds on R for some graph classes; per excerpts, Corollary 20 and Theorem 25 are general lower bounds, but their statements were not read. Whether either applies to general graphs at order n above floor(n/2) is not established by anything I could read.
events.remains: Unknown. If either lower bound applied to general graphs and exceeded floor(n/2) at some order, the question would be settled as yes; the statements have to be read to know.
events.doubts: The statements of Corollary 20 and Theorem 25 were not read, so their scope (general graphs or specific classes) is unknown. The abstract's claim of settling open problems is about existence and length for classes; the record does not tie any of those to floor(n/2).
events.direction: Not established. Lower bounds could cut either way on this question, so the record cannot say.

events.what_happened: Hefty, Horn, Muir and Owens, 'Word-representation numbers of graphs: Bottlenecks and bounds', Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 223 (2026) 106215, DOI 10.1016/j.jcta.2026.106215 (open access per search excerpt). The ScienceDirect page refused the fetch (HTTP 403), so the following is from a search-result summary: the paper focuses on lower bounds on word-representation length; it proves a sharp lower bound on R for almost every balanced bipartite graph, and a non-trivial lower bound for the hypercube; the results depend on the interplay between poset dimension and word-representations; the multi-word-representation number can be unbounded, refuting a conjecture of Kenkireth and Malhotra (using the resolution of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for C5); and there is an edit-distance result (cut off in the excerpt).
events.revisions: Online-first date not found; listed in the October 2026 issue per search excerpt. Month omitted because the first public date could not be pinned.
events.delivers: Per the excerpt: lower bounds for almost every balanced bipartite graph (of order about N/4 for N = 2n, by my reading of a garbled formula) and for the hypercube. Nothing reported for general graphs in the excerpt.
events.remains: General graphs, and whether any graph on n vertices exceeds floor(n/2).

disputes.summary: The general upper bound on R for n-vertex word-representable graphs is stated as n in the 2008 preprint (arXiv:0810.0310), as 2n in the 2015 preprint and 2016 journal version (arXiv:1501.07108), and as 2(n − κ(G)) (≤ 2n − 4 for non-complete graphs) in secondary sources citing the 2016 paper. No account of the change was found, and the 2008 PDF was not readable.

The bipartite conjecture (R ≤ n/4 for bipartite graphs on n vertices, or ⌈(m+n)/4⌉ in the Glen et al. form) is attributed to no one in the 2021 abstract, and to Glen et al. in the 2025 follow-up. The Glen et al. paper (2016) was not read on this point.

summary: Searches (47 web searches) and about 30 page fetches found no counterexample and no proof of the floor(n/2) bound for general graphs in any source up to 11 October 2026. The benchmark is set by older results. Halldórsson, Kitaev and Pyatkin give an n/2 family (per the 2008 abstract and 2015 abstract; the family itself is the crown graph with an added all-adjacent vertex according to excerpts, which has odd order 2k+1 and R = k, so it meets floor(n/2) exactly at odd n; I found no graph in the record that reaches n/2 at even n, which is my inference from the cited families and not a stated result). Their upper bound is n in the 2008 preprint and 2n in 2015/2016, and Wikipedia cites 2(n − κ) ≤ 2n − 4. Glen, Kitaev and Pyatkin (2016) show that crowns have R = ⌈n/2⌉ on 2n vertices, far below the threshold. Akgün et al. (2018) computed representation numbers for graphs up to 9 vertices and found R ≤ 4 there (per excerpts; the per-n maxima were not read). Since 26 January 2024, the bullet has these events: Mozhui and Krishna (1 June 2025) bound bipartite R by 1 + ⌈m/2⌉ with m the smaller part, settling the Glen et al. bipartite conjecture except for equal even parts; Colbrook and Drysdale (24 September 2026) prove every bipartite graph on N ≥ 9 vertices has R ≤ ⌈N/4⌉, so no bipartite graph on N ≥ 9 is a counterexample, and with the 2025 bound, none on N ≥ 4 by my arithmetic; Hefty, Horn, Muir and Owens published lower-bound papers in EJC (4 Oct 2024) and JCTA (2026) whose full texts I could not read, so whether any general lower bound exceeds floor(n/2) is open to me. Close calls. (a) Colbrook and Drysdale is a class restriction (bipartite only), so under §2.1 it does not resolve the bullet; I record it as a restricted case. (b) The authors' AI declaration says the approach 'arose through discussions' with ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6, that the obstruction classification 'emerged from discussions' with ChatGPT 5.6, that further discussions with ChatGPT 6 addressed the odd part sizes, and that ChatGPT 5.6 through Codex assisted with counting and the finite certificates. On §5.4 these look load-bearing, not proofreading; the verbatim quotes were read through a fetch that enforced length limits, so the middle sentences should be checked against the PDF. The first and last quotes were confirmed verbatim across two fetches. (c) The literal existential reading is trivially yes at n = 1 (K1 has R = 1 > floor(1/2) = 0) and at n = 3 (the path P3 is a non-complete circle graph with R = 2 > floor(3/2) = 1). If non-word-representable graphs count as needing more copies, W5 (6 vertices, the smallest non-word-representable graph) also qualifies. No source frames the bullet this way; the record flags it so the later pass can choose. (d) The 2008 preprint's upper bound n conflicts with the 2n bound from the same authors in 2015; I could not resolve which the authors stand behind.
competing_reading: The bullet is open for general graphs, and the bipartite class is closed: a reader who takes the question to mean large n, and who counts Colbrook and Drysdale as the bipartite half of a result the community was working toward, records 'open, bipartite case closed'. A reader who takes the bullet literally, as an existential over all n, records 'yes' at trivial small n (K1, P3) or, counting non-word-representable graphs, at n ≥ 6. Neither reading changes the general-graph status found here. A third reader could argue that the Hefty–Horn–Muir–Owens lower bounds, if they apply to general graphs, already exceed floor(n/2) at some order, which would make the general question answered 'yes' in the window; I could not read the statements to rule this out, so this reading is not excluded.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Hefty, Horn, Muir and Owens (EJC 31(4) #P4.2, Corollary 20 and Theorem 25; and JCTA 223 (2026) 106215) to see whether any lower bound applies to general graphs and exceeds floor(n/2) at some order. (2) The per-n maxima tables of Akgün, Gent, Kitaev and Zantema (2019), for n ≤ 9, to check the threshold for each n up to 9, and any extension to n = 10 and 11. (3) A construction of a graph on some n with R > floor(n/2), or a general upper bound below floor(n/2), either of which would settle the existential. (4) The Kitaev–Lozin book's Chapter 7 wording and the Kitaev survey's Section 9, to confirm the original formulation and whether the question is posed for all n or for large n. (5) The Colbrook–Drysdale PDF's declaration section read verbatim, and the Lean repository's files with a #print axioms check on the main theorems, to settle the AI and sorry-free status in event colbrook-drysdale-2026.
